mainTopic: The משואות for ראש חודש: why they were lit only after a חסר month, the kinds of cedar used, and related אגדות
overview: This amud continues the discussion of the signal fires (משואות) that told distant communities when בית דין had declared ראש חודש. The גמרא explains why the fires were lit only after a חסר month. Lighting for both kinds of months would confuse people when a fire was delayed to מוצאי שבת. Skipping the fire on ערב שבת also fails, because people might think it was missed by accident. Lighting only for a מלא month fails too, says אביי, because it would cost people two days of work. Next the גמרא explains the cedar poles of the משנה: רב יהודה counts four kinds of ארזים, and the school of רב counts ten, seven from a פסוק in ישעיה plus three more. This leads to side discussions about coral, the great ship used to harvest it, and three teachings of רבי יוחנן about the trees of the פסוק and about רבי עקיבא and his colleagues. Finally the גמרא returns to the משנה and asks what בית בלתין is, and רב's answer begins on the next amud.

steps.title: Lighting for both kinds of months would cause confusion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes explaining why משואות were not lit for both a חסר and a מלא month. If ראש חודש fell on ערב שבת, the fire would be delayed to מוצאי שבת, and people would not know what the delayed fire meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: [People would come] to err. They would say: 'This month is חסר, and the reason they didn't light yesterday is that it was impossible [because of שבת].' Or perhaps it is מלא, and they lit at its proper time.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an answer that started on the previous amud. It explains why lighting fires for every month, both חסר and מלא, would lead to mistakes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose ראש חודש fell on ערב שבת. The fires could not be lit that night because it was שבת, so they would be lit on מוצאי שבת instead. Someone who sees a fire on מוצאי שבת cannot tell whether it is a late fire for a חסר month or an on-time fire for a מלא month. So the signal would fail to tell people the real date.

keyTerms.meaning: To make a mistake, to be misled

steps.confusionAlert: These fires are lit for the new month's ראש חודש. Whether the old month was חסר or מלא decides which day is ראש חודש. The fire is lit on the night after the day that was declared ראש חודש.

phrases.english: [people would come] to err — they would say:
phrases.notes: Continues a sentence that began on the previous amud.

phrases.english: This month is deficient (29 days),
and the reason they didn't light it yesterday
is because it was impossible (it was שבת).
Or perhaps it is a full (30-day) month,
and they lit it at its proper time.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes an answer that began on the previous amud.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Lighting for both חסר and מלא months would be a fuller signal.
steps.terutzMaskana: A fire delayed to מוצאי שבת could be read two ways, so lighting for both kinds of months would mislead people.

steps.title: Suggestion: light for both, but skip when ראש חודש is on ערב שבת
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a fix. Light for both kinds of months, and when ראש חודש falls on ערב שבת, do not light at all. People would then understand that a missing fire means the month was חסר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let them light for both a מלא and a חסר month. When ראש חודש falls on ערב שבת, let them not light at all. Since we don't light on מוצאי שבת, and we normally light for a מלא month, people will know it is חסר!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back with a clever workaround that seems to solve the problem from Step 1.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea is to never light on מוצאי שבת, so there is never a confusing delayed fire. In this plan fires are normally lit for every month. So if a whole cycle passes with no fire, people could work out that this must be the ערב שבת exception, which means a חסר month. If that works, the reason given in Step 1 for lighting only after חסר months falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: And let them do it (a suggestion)

phrases.english: But let them light both for a full and for a deficient month,

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מִקְּלַע רֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ בְּעֶרֶב שַׁבָּת
phrases.english: and when the New Moon happens to fall on Friday,
let them not light at all.
And since we don't light on Saturday night,
and we do light for a full month —
people will surely know that it is deficient!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the confusion argument of Step 1 by offering a way around it.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that lighting for both kinds of months must cause confusion
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If no fire is ever lit on מוצאי שבת, there is no delayed fire to misread, and the missing fire itself becomes a clear signal of a חסר month.

steps.title: People would think the fires were missed by accident
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that even so, people could still err. They might assume the month was מלא and that the fires were simply not lit because something prevented it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even so, they would come to err. They would say: 'This month is מלא, and the reason they didn't light is that they were prevented by circumstances beyond their control.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the workaround from Step 2.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Under the Step 2 plan, a missing fire is supposed to mean 'חסר month on ערב שבת.' But people far away might explain the missing fire another way: something went wrong and the fire-lighters could not do their job. Silence is not a reliable signal, because it can always be blamed on an accident.

keyTerms.meaning: Being prevented by circumstances beyond one's control (אונס)

phrases.english: Even so, they would come to err,
saying: This month is full,
and the reason they didn't light —
is that they were prevented by circumstances beyond their control.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Practical concern (an alternative explanation for the missing signal)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A missing fire would clearly mean 'חסר month on ערב שבת.'
steps.terutzMaskana: People might blame the missing fire on an accident, so confusion remains.

steps.title: Why not light only for a full month?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: then do the opposite. Light only after a מלא month and never after a חסר month.
steps.simpleTranslation: Then let them light for a מלא month, and not light for a חסר month at all!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a new question that challenges the משנה's choice to signal חסר months rather than מלא months.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If signaling only one kind of month is the best system, nothing yet shows why it must be the חסר month. Signaling the מלא month seems just as workable. So the גמרא wants a reason for picking חסר.

phrases.english: Then let them light for a full month,
and not light for a deficient month at all!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלֶיעְבֵּיד אַמָּלֵא, וְלָא לֶיעְבֵּיד אַחָסֵר כְּלָל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts that only one kind of month should be signaled, and now asks why it is the חסר one.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that fires are lit only after a חסר month
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Signaling only מלא months would also avoid the ערב שבת confusion, so why choose חסר?

steps.title: אביי: signaling only full months would idle people for two days
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that lighting only for a מלא month would make people stop work for two days every month. That is ביטול מלאכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: Because of the loss of work for the people for two days.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי gives the final reason why the fires signal a חסר month and not a מלא month.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People held back from certain work on ראש חודש, so on the 30th they had to treat the day as a possible ראש חודש. When fires signal a חסר month, a fire that night tells people the 30th was ראש חודש, and they can go back to work the next day. If fires signaled only מלא months, people would always have to stay idle on both the 30th and the 31st before they could know the answer.
steps.whatToRemember: משואות were lit only after a חסר month. Lighting for both kinds of months fails because a fire delayed to מוצאי שבת is ambiguous. Skipping the fire when ראש חודש falls on ערב שבת fails because people may think the fire was missed by accident. Signaling only מלא months fails because of a two-day ביטול מלאכה (אביי).
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that חז"ל designed public systems to avoid confusion and also to avoid needless loss of people's livelihood.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Because of the loss of work
for the people for two days.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: מִשּׁוּם בִּיטּוּל מְלָאכָה לָעָם שְׁנֵי יָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 4.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Signaling only מלא months would work just as well as signaling חסר months.
steps.terutzMaskana: Signaling only מלא months would always cause two idle days, so the fires signal חסר months.

steps.title: Quoting the משנה on how the signal fires were lit
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the line of the משנה that describes how the משואות were lit.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: How did they light the signal fires? They brought long poles, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a new line from the משנה. This is a setup line that opens the next discussion, which is about the wood used for these poles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The full משנה says the poles were made of ארז (cedar) and other materials that burn well. The word כּוּ׳ ("etc.") tells us to remember the rest of the line, which mentions cedar wood. That word ארז is what the next steps will discuss.

keyTerms.meaning: Signal fires or torches lit on mountaintops to announce ראש חודש
They would light (raise up) the fires
"Etc.": the quote continues in the source

phrases.english: How would they light the signal fires?
They would bring long poles, etc.
phrases.notes: The משנה continues: "of cedar", along with other materials that burn well

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the debate about why fires were lit only for a חסר month, to the next line of the משנה about how they were lit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The משנה describes the משואות as being made from long poles, including cedar wood.

steps.title: רב יהודה: there are four kinds of cedar
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה lists four kinds of trees that count as ארזים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: There are four kinds of cedar: ארז, קתרום, עץ שמן, and ברוש.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה explains the word ארז from the משנה. He says it covers four kinds of trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the poles were made of ארז. רב יהודה teaches that ארז is a family name for four species, so any of these four would work. Only one of them, קתרום, is an unfamiliar name, so the גמרא will explain it next.

keyTerms.meaning: A type of cedar tree (identified in the next step)

steps.confusionAlert: Here ארז is used in two ways. It is the name of one specific tree, and it is also the name of the whole family of four trees. The specific ארז is one member of the family.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
there are four kinds of cedar:
cedar, katrom, the oil tree (pine), and cypress.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה, אַרְבָּעָה מִינֵי אֲרָזִים הֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the word ארז from the משנה just quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The category ארז includes four species: ארז, קתרום, עץ שמן, and ברוש.

steps.title: Identifying the tree called קתרום
steps.stepSummary: Different opinions identify קתרום by its everyday Aramaic name.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is קתרום? רב said: it is the אדרא tree. The school of רבי שילא said: it is the מבליגא tree. And some say: it is the גולמיש tree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the unfamiliar name קתרום by giving the local names people knew.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a translation question, not a legal argument. Three opinions give three different local tree names for קתרום. None of them changes the rule. They only help identify the tree.

keyTerms.meaning: Local name of a tree (רב's identification of קתרום)
The school (study hall) of רבי שילא
"And some say it": an alternate version

phrases.english: Katrom: Rav said it is the addera tree.
The school of Rabbi Sheila says: it is the mavliga tree,
and some say: this is the gulmish tree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains one of the four tree names from רב יהודה's list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: קתרום is identified as אדרא (according to רב), מבליגא (according to the school of רבי שילא), or גולמיש (according to some).

steps.title: The school of רב counts ten kinds of cedar from a verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that רבה בר רב הונא, quoting the school of רב, disagrees and counts ten kinds of cedar based on a פסוק in ישעיה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with רבה בר רב הונא. He said that the school of רב says: There are ten kinds of cedar. As it says: "I will place in the wilderness the cedar, the acacia, the myrtle, and the oil tree. I will set in the desert the cypress, the plane tree, and the box tree together."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a second opinion that argues with רב יהודה. This opinion says there are ten kinds of cedar, not four.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה counted four kinds. The school of רב counts ten, and brings a פסוק that lists trees together as one group. The idea is that every tree in this פסוק belongs to the cedar family.

keyTerms.meaning: "And it disagrees": this opinion argues with the previous one
"They say in the school of רב"
Two trees from the פסוק (plane/maple and box tree)

phrases.english: And this disagrees with Rabba bar Rav Huna.
For Rabba bar Rav Huna said,
they say in the school of Rav:
there are ten kinds of cedar,
as it is said: "I will place in the wilderness the cedar,
the acacia, and the myrtle, and the oil tree;
I will set in the desert the cypress,
the plane tree and the box tree together."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents an opinion that argues with רב יהודה's count of four.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the school of רב, there are ten kinds of cedar, learned from the trees grouped together in ישעיה 41:19.

steps.title: Translating the seven trees of the verse
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives the everyday Aramaic name for each tree in the פסוק.
steps.simpleTranslation: ארז is ארזא. שטה is תורניתא. הדס is אסא. עץ שמן is אפרסמא. ברוש is ברתא. תדהר is שאגא. תאשור is שוריבנא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא translates each tree in the פסוק into the Aramaic name people used every day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a word list that matches the Biblical name to the local name. It helps us count the trees, and the count is what sets up the question in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Aramaic name given for עץ שמן (often understood as balsam)

phrases.english: Cedar is arza; acacia is turnita;
myrtle is asa; the oil tree is afarsema;
cypress is berata; the plane tree is shaga;
the box tree is shurivna.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Translates the trees named in the פסוק just quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each of the seven trees in the פסוק is matched with its local Aramaic name.

steps.title: But these are only seven
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the פסוק names only seven trees, not ten.
steps.simpleTranslation: But these are only seven!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא counts the trees in the פסוק and finds only seven. So how can the school of רב say there are ten?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The claim was ten kinds, and the פסוק was brought as the source. The source gives only seven, so three are missing. The claim does not match its own proof.

keyTerms.meaning: "These are seven!": a challenge pointing out that the count is short

phrases.english: These are only seven!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the count of ten in light of the seven trees just listed.
steps.kashyaTarget: The school of רב's statement that there are ten kinds of cedar
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק given as the source lists only seven trees, so the number ten is not supported.

steps.title: רב דימי reports three more kinds
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports that three more trees were added to the seven, and the גמרא gives their local names.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came from ארץ ישראל, he said: They added to them אלונים, אלמונים, and אלמוגין. אלונים are בוטמי, אלמונים are בלוטי, and אלמוגין are כסיתא.
steps.whatsHappening: רב דימי answers the question by naming three more trees that bring the count up to ten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seven from the פסוק are not the full list. The חכמים added three more trees to the cedar family, which makes ten. The גמרא then translates the three new names into local Aramaic.

keyTerms.meaning: "When רב דימי came" from ארץ ישראל to בבל, bringing teachings with him

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:
They added to them
terebinths, oaks, and coral wood.
Terebinths are butmei; oaks are balutei;
coral wood is kasita.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי, אָמַר: הוֹסִיפוּ עֲלֵיהֶם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא that only seven trees were listed.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adds missing items: three more species complete the count of ten.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ten kinds must all come from the פסוק, which lists only seven.
steps.terutzMaskana: Seven come from the פסוק, and three more (אלונים, אלמונים, אלמוגין) were added, for a total of ten.

steps.title: Another version of the three added trees
steps.stepSummary: An alternate version gives a different list of the three added trees, along with their local names.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say the three added trees are ארונים, ערמונים, and אלמוגין. ארונים are ערי, ערמונים are דולבי, and אלמוגין are כסיתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of רב דימי's answer, with a slightly different list of the three extra trees.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions agree that three trees were added and that אלמוגין is one of them. They differ on the other two: this version has ארונים and ערמונים instead of אלונים and אלמונים.

keyTerms.meaning: "There are those who say": an alternate version of the teaching
A tree, often identified as the bay or laurel (local name: עָרֵי)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two views on how many kinds of ארזים there are. רב יהודה says four. The school of רב says ten: seven from the פסוק in ישעיה plus three more, and the exact identity of those three is disputed.

phrases.english: There are those who say:
bay trees, plane trees, and coral wood.
Bay trees are arei; plane trees are dulvei;
coral wood is kasita.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternate version of רב דימי's list of three added trees.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Alternate version of the same answer
steps.terutzMaskana: The three added trees are ארונים, ערמונים, and אלמוגין.

steps.title: רב explains the mighty ship in the verse
steps.stepSummary: Since coral was just mentioned, the גמרא brings רב's explanation that צי אדיר means a great ship.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: "And a mighty ship shall not pass through it." רב said: This is a great ship (בורני).
steps.whatsHappening: This is a short side point. Because coral wood was just mentioned, the גמרא quotes רב explaining a phrase in a פסוק about a great ship.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק in ישעיה describes a river so wide that even a צי אדיר could not cross it. רב identifies this as a large ship called a בורני. It appears right after אלמוגין because, as the next steps describe, this kind of great ship is used to gather coral from the sea.

phrases.english: "And a mighty ship shall not pass through it":
Rav said: This is a great ship (burnei).

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A side point linked to the mention of coral wood (אלמוגין).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: צי אדיר in the פסוק refers to a great ship called a בורני.

steps.title: How do they collect the coral?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the coral is actually gathered with the great ship.
steps.simpleTranslation: How do they do it?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short practical question: how do people actually harvest coral? This is a setup line that prepares the description in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 mentioned the great ship used for coral. Now the גמרא wants to know how that ship is used. This is a request for information, not an attack on anything.

phrases.english: How do they do it?
phrases.notes: Asks how the coral is collected.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks how the great ship from step 14 is used to collect coral.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical method for harvesting coral.

steps.title: The method for pulling coral from the sea
steps.stepSummary: Workers sink a sand-filled ship, a diver ties the coral to it, and then they dump the sand so the rising ship pulls the coral loose.
steps.simpleTranslation: They bring six thousand men for twelve months of the year, and some say twelve thousand men for six months of the year. They load the ship with sand until it sinks. A diver goes down and ties flax ropes around the coral, and ties the ropes to the ship. Then they throw the sand overboard, and as the ship rises it rips the coral out and brings it up.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by describing the coral-harvesting process step by step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two opinions on the workforce: 6,000 men for a full year, or 12,000 men for half a year. Either way the labor is the same. The method uses the ship's weight. Sand sinks it, and dumping the sand makes it float back up. That upward pull tears the coral off the sea floor.

phrases.english: They bring six thousand men
for the twelve months of the year,
and some say
phrases.notes: Introduces a second opinion on the workforce.

phrases.english: twelve thousand men
for six months of the year,
and they load it (the ship) with sand until it sinks.
And a diver goes down
and ties flax ropes around the coral,
and ties them to the ship.
Then they take the sand and throw it overboard,
and as it rises, it uproots the coral and brings it up.
phrases.notes: The rising ship pulls the coral free.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַיְיתוּ שֵׁית אַלְפֵי גַּבְרֵי בִּתְרֵיסַר יַרְחֵי שַׁתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ship is sunk with sand, the coral is tied to it, and then the sand is dumped so the rising ship rips the coral loose.

steps.title: Coral is worth double its weight in silver
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא notes that coral trades for twice its weight in silver.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is exchanged for twice its weight in silver.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a side fact: coral is extremely valuable.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why so much effort goes into harvesting it. Thousands of workers and months of labor are worth it because one measure of coral trades for two measures of silver.

phrases.english: And it is exchanged for two times its weight in silver.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a fact about the value of the coral just described.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Coral is worth twice its weight in silver.

steps.title: The three ports for coral and pearls
steps.stepSummary: There are three ports. The two Roman ones bring up coral, and the Persian one brings up pearls and is called the royal port.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are three ports: two belong to the Romans and one to the Persians. The Roman ones bring up coral; the Persian one brings up pearls, and it is called the royal port.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds more background about where coral and pearls are taken out of the sea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is still a side note on the coral topic. It tells us who controls the ports and what each port produces. The Persian port has a special name because of its royal status.

phrases.english: There are three ports:
two belonging to the Romans
and one belonging to the Persians.
Those of the Romans bring up coral,
that of the Persians brings up pearls,
and it is called: the royal port.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the background on coral by describing the ports.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two Roman ports produce coral, and one Persian royal port produces pearls.

steps.title: Every acacia taken from Jerusalem will be returned
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that הקדוש ברוך הוא will return to ירושלים every שיטה tree the nations took. He learns this from the פסוק of trees, reading מדבר as ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Every single acacia tree that the nations took from ירושלים, הקדוש ברוך הוא will return to it, as it says: 'I will plant in the wilderness the cedar, the acacia.' And 'wilderness' means only ירושלים, as it says: 'ציון has become a wilderness.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the פסוק of the trees. רבי יוחנן uses it to teach a promise about the future of ירושלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק says ה׳ will plant trees in the מדבר. רבי יוחנן proves from another פסוק that ציון is called a מדבר. So the promise of planting trees in the מדבר becomes a promise to restore the trees taken from ירושלים.
steps.whyThisMatters: It ties the list of trees in ישעיהו back to the future rebuilding of ירושלים.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Each and every acacia tree
that the nations took from Jerusalem,
the Holy One, Blessed be He, will in the future
return them to it,
as it says: 'I will place in the wilderness the cedar, the acacia,'
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 41:19, the פסוק of the trees.

phrases.english: and 'wilderness' means nothing other than Jerusalem,
as it says: 'Zion has become a wilderness, etc.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כׇּל שִׁיטָּה וְשִׁיטָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the coral side topic and returns to the פסוק of the trees.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All the acacia trees taken from ירושלים will be restored to it by ה׳.

steps.title: Learning without teaching is like a myrtle in the wilderness
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן teaches that one who learns תורה but does not teach it is like a הדס in the מדבר.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Anyone who learns תורה and does not teach it is like a myrtle in the wilderness.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן gives another teaching connected to the trees of the פסוק, this time about the הדס.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A הדס smells wonderful, but in the מדבר nobody is there to enjoy it. In the same way, תורה that a person keeps to himself does not benefit anyone else. This is a criticism of learning without teaching.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Anyone who learns Torah and does not teach it,
is like a myrtle in the wilderness.
phrases.notes: Its fragrance is wasted with no one to enjoy it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: כׇּל הַלּוֹמֵד תּוֹרָה וְאֵינוֹ מְלַמְּדָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second teaching from רבי יוחנן, based on the הדס in the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Learning תורה without teaching it is like a fragrant הדס wasted in the מדבר.

steps.title: Another version: teaching where there are no scholars is precious
steps.stepSummary: Another version reads רבי יוחנן positively. One who learns and teaches תורה where there are no תלמידי חכמים is like a הדס in the מדבר, which is especially precious.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: Anyone who learns תורה and teaches it in a place where there are no תלמידי חכמים is like a myrtle in the wilderness, which is precious.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different version of רבי יוחנן's comparison that turns it into praise.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the point is that a הדס in the מדבר is rare, so people treasure it. A person who teaches תורה where there are no scholars is just as valued. The same picture is used, but it means the opposite.
steps.confusionAlert: Both versions use the same image of a הדס in the מדבר, but with opposite meanings. In the first version it is wasted, a criticism. In the second it is treasured, a praise.
steps.whatToRemember: The image of a הדס in the מדבר can mean wasted fragrance (learning without teaching) or rare preciousness (teaching where there are no scholars).

phrases.english: There are those who say:
Anyone who learns Torah and teaches it
in a place where there are no Torah scholars —
is like a myrtle in the wilderness, which is precious.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְאָמְרִי: כׇּל הַלּוֹמֵד תּוֹרָה וּמְלַמְּדָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives an alternate version of step 20 that turns the comparison into praise.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Teaching תורה where there are no scholars is precious, like a rare הדס in the מדבר.

steps.title: Woe to the nations, who have no way to repair their sin
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says the nations have no remedy for what they did to ישראל. He brings a פסוק showing that in the future every stolen material will be replaced with something more valuable.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן said: Woe to the nations, for they have no remedy. As it says: 'Instead of copper I will bring gold, instead of iron I will bring silver, instead of wood copper, and instead of stones iron.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן makes a new statement: the nations have no way to fix the harm they did. He quotes a פסוק about exchanging lesser materials for better ones.
steps.deeperAnalysis: On its own the פסוק sounds like good news: anything stolen can be replaced, even with something better. So it shows that material losses can always be made up. That is the setup for רבי יוחנן's real point in the next step, about what can never be replaced.

keyTerms.meaning: Remedy, a way to fix or repair

steps.confusionAlert: The פסוק does not prove that the nations have no remedy. It proves the opposite for material things. The 'no remedy' only comes from the question in the next step: what could replace רבי עקיבא?

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Woe to the nations,
for they have no remedy,
as it is stated:
'Instead of copper I will bring gold,
and instead of iron I will bring silver,
and instead of wood, copper,
and instead of stones, iron.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: אוֹי לָהֶם לַגּוֹיִם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another statement in the series from רבי יוחנן. It follows the theme of step 19, where הקדוש ברוך הוא restores what the nations took from ירושלים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Material things the nations took will be repaid with better materials, but the nations still have no full remedy for their sins.

steps.title: Nothing can replace רבי עקיבא and his colleagues
steps.stepSummary: Material things can be exchanged, but nothing can be brought in place of רבי עקיבא and his colleagues, whom the nations killed. A פסוק in יואל says their blood will not be forgiven.
steps.simpleTranslation: But in place of רבי עקיבא and his colleagues, what can they bring? And about them it says: 'I will clear them, but their blood I will not clear.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן finishes his point. The killing of רבי עקיבא and the other martyrs can never be paid back, and he brings a פסוק from יואל to back this up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question 'what can they bring?' is not really asking for an answer. It means nothing in the world is worth as much as these צדיקים. The פסוק in יואל confirms it: other sins may be cleared, but the spilled blood will not be cleared. That is why the nations 'have no remedy.'

keyTerms.meaning: רבי עקיבא and his colleagues, the sages killed by the Romans (the עשרה הרוגי מלכות)
What can they bring? (a rhetorical question meaning: nothing)
And I will clear, hold innocent

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's lesson: stolen property can be repaid, even with something better, but the lives of צדיקים like רבי עקיבא can never be replaced. That is why the nations have no full remedy.

phrases.english: In place of Rabbi Akiva and his colleagues,
what can they bring!
phrases.notes: A rhetorical exclamation: there is nothing that could be brought.

phrases.english: And about them it says:
'And I will clear them, but their blood I will not clear.'

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּחַת רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא וַחֲבֵירָיו מַאי מְבִיאִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the exchange pattern of the פסוק in step 22 to show what cannot be exchanged, and adds a supporting פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's claim that the nations have no remedy
steps.raayaSupportSource: The פסוק 'וְנִקֵּיתִי דָּמָם לֹא נִקֵּיתִי' (יואל), read as referring to the blood of the martyrs

steps.title: Back to the משנה: what is בית בלתין?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה about which mountains the torches were lit on to announce the new month. It asks what the last place mentioned, בית בלתין, is. רב begins to answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'From where would they light the torches… and from בית בלתין.' What is בית בלתין? רב said:
steps.whatsHappening: The אגדה is over, and the גמרא goes back to the משנה. It quotes the list of torch mountains and asks what the place called בית בלתין is. The line ends with 'רב said:', which sets up his answer on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed a chain of mountain tops where fires were lit to tell distant communities that בית דין had declared the new month. The chain ended at בית בלתין, an unfamiliar name, so the גמרא asks what it is. This is a plain question of identification, not a challenge.

keyTerms.meaning: Lighting torches or fire signals on mountain tops to announce ראש חודש
Etc.; shows that only part of the משנה is being quoted
The last station in the torch-signal chain

steps.confusionAlert: The quoted words are not new statements. They are a shortened quote of the משנה, with 'כו׳' standing in for the missing middle stations. רב's answer continues on the next amud.

phrases.english: [The משנה said:] 'And from where would they light the torches, etc.'
phrases.notes: The skipped stations are הר המשחה, סרטבא, גריפינא, and חוורן.

phrases.english: 'and from Beit Biltin.'
What is Beit Biltin?
Rav said:
phrases.notes: The answer continues on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the aggadic series of רבי יוחנן and returns to explaining the משנה about the torch signals.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The identity or meaning of the place name בית בלתין in the משנה
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב's answer is introduced here but appears on the next amud.
